power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world's population and causes most cases of gastric cancer worldwide, yet fundamental questions about its within-host genetic diversity remain unresolved.
Decades of work on Hp genomics depends on culturing clinical isolates, which can distort within-host genetic heterogeneity that informs Hp virulence and antimicrobial resistance.

Culture-free alternatives have been limited by the extremely low Hp abundance in gastric tissue (usually 10 -3 to 10 -7 of total genomic DNA), making direct metagenomics prohibitively expensive and existing enrichment strategies insufficient for whole-genome.

Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world's population and is the leading infectious cause of gastric cancer 1 , the fifth most common cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death worldwide 2 .
text.formatted: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world's population and is the leading infectious cause of gastric cancer 1 , the fifth most common cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Hp strains differ markedly in their capacity to cause disease, driven by variation in key virulence loci: the cag pathogenicity island, cagA EPIYA configuration, vacA alleles, and adhesin repertoires that together determine the intensity of host interaction and the risk of malignant progression [3] [4] [5] .
text.formatted: Hp strains differ markedly in their capacity to cause disease, driven by variation in key virulence loci: the cag pathogenicity island, cagA EPIYA configuration, vacA alleles, and adhesin repertoires that together determine the intensity of host interaction and the risk of malignant progression <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> .

text.text: Identifying patients at highest risk therefore depends on knowing the virulence configuration of the strain they carry.

Importantly, selecting an effective eradication regimen requires knowing the strain's antibiotic resistance genotype [6] [7] [8] , as rising antimicrobial resistance has driven first-line treatment success below 90% in most regions, as low as 60% for certain antibiotics in certain regions [9] [10] [11] [12] .
text.formatted: Importantly, selecting an effective eradication regimen requires knowing the strain's antibiotic resistance genotype <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> , as rising antimicrobial resistance has driven first-line treatment success below 90% in most regions, as low as 60% for certain antibiotics in certain regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> .

text.text: Despite four decades of Hp genomic research, this information cannot be efficiently obtained for individual patients in clinical practice.
The barrier is technical rather than conceptual.
Hp is exceptionally diverse and individual strains evolve within hosts over years 13 , making whole-genome resolution essential for reliable biological and clinical inference.
text.formatted: Hp is exceptionally diverse and individual strains evolve within hosts over years <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , making whole-genome resolution essential for reliable biological and clinical inference.

text.text: Nearly all Hp genomic insight has come from culture of clinical isolates.

However, culture introduces bias by favoring strains that grow better under laboratory conditions, collapses complex multi-strain infections to a single strain, misses single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and structural variations (SVs), and misrepresents the genomic landscape of Hp as it exists at the gastric mucosa.

Culture-free alternatives have been attempted, but each is bounded by the fundamental challenge of the Hp scarcity of Hp in gastric tissue: Hp constitutes only 10 -3 to 10 -7 of total genomic DNA, with the vast majority derived from human cells 14, 15 .

text.text: Here we report uHp-seq, a culture-free workflow that reconstructs Hp genomes directly from host-dominated clinical specimens by coupling methylation-guided depletion of non-Hp DNA with ultra-low-input sequencing optimized for the trace quantities of the enriched Hp DNA that remain. uHp-seq achieves a thousand-fold enrichment and recovers near-complete genomes from gastric biopsies and minimally invasive gastric string samples across a wide range of Hp abundance.

We show that culture systematically misrepresents within-host Hp heterogeneity, missing mixed infections, collapsing co-existing cagA EPIYA variants with distinct oncogenic potential, and flattening gastric regional Hp genomic structure.
In contrast, uHp-seq resolves these heterogeneity.
Genome-wide profiling of antibiotic resistance variants via uHpseq outperforms PCR-based and probe-based commercial panels.

Applied to gastric string samples from patients with refractory infections, uHp-seq delivers comprehensive antibiotic resistance profiles without endoscopy, establishing a practical route to genome-guided eradication therapy.

text.text: For AMR-associated variants, the diagnostic gap is created by limited locus coverage of PCR as well as primer failure with highly variable resistance genes.

uHp-seq enables highly sensitive, culture-free recovery of Hp genomes directly from clinical specimens, yielding near-complete genomes from biopsies and minimally invasive string samples.

By recovering Hp genomes as they exist in vivo, uHp-seq opens new opportunities to study the native biology of Hp host interaction and within-host adaptation that culture has obscured, while also enabling more precise and scalable genome-guided eradication therapy.

text.text: Beyond individual loci, within-host strain heterogeneity is substantially more complex than previously appreciated: mixed infections, regional structuring along the proximaldistal axis of the stomach, and individual informative loci such as cagA that harbor up to four distinct configurations within a single patient.
In addition, uHp-seq identified truncating variants in multiple genes related to TonB-dependent iron and nickel acquisition that were absent from the corresponding cultured isolates.

Because Hp encodes multiple TonB-ExbB-ExbD systems and FrpB/FecA-family transporters with potential functional redundancy 65 , disruption of individual components may attenuate rather than abolish metal acquisition, potentially reflecting adaptation to the nutrient landscape of the gastric niche.

These findings argue that core questions of Hp population structure, host adaptation, and within-host evolution should be revisited with culture-free genomic approaches.

For virulence genotyping, uHp-seq has important advantages over existing approaches: it captures the in vivo virulence landscape that culture distorts, and it resolves full locus configurations including the intact ~40 kb cagPAI, structural variants within cagA, and the highly variable adhesin repertoire, which PCR panels do not reliably cover.

In addition, given that EPIYA-C copy number is associated with CagA activity 66 , uHp-seq reliably resolved EPIYA-C copy-number variation that was missed by probe based target-enrichment due to hybridization biases.

text.text: The most striking virulence finding is that individual hosts simultaneously harbor multiple co-existing cagA EPIYA variants with distinct oncogenic potential, a within-host heterogeneity that culture collapses to a single dominant type.

EPIYA configuration is a primary determinant of CagA-mediated oncogenic signaling through SHP-2 67 , and the co-existence of variants with distinct oncogenic potential within a single host means that culture-based EPIYA typing misrepresents the true virulence landscape of the infection.

text.text: Taken together, these findings indicate that the full virulence landscape of Hp, across cagPAI, EPIYA configuration, adhesins, and strain identity, has been assessed through a culture-distorted lens, and that uHpseq provides the substrate to revisit it.

For AMR-associated variants, our study showed that the diagnostic gap here owes to the restricted locus coverage of commercial PCR and probe panels, as well as primer failure on highly variable resistance genes. uHp-seq genome-wide recovery outperforms targeted PCR panels for AMX and MNZ specifically, where resistance is determined by variants distributed across full gene sequences rather than a small number of canonical hotspots.
Reliable determination of AMX susceptibility is increasingly important with the introduction of . vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy as a first-line treatment option 37, 70 .

text.text: This regimen uses a single antibiotic, reduces exposure to other antibiotics, and is generally well tolerated.
Because its efficacy relies directly on AMX activity, accurate detection of AMX resistance before treatment could help guide appropriate use and avoid treatment failure.

For CLR and LEV, where resistance is dominated by a handful of well-characterized mutations, targeted panels perform equivalently, confirming that whole-genome recovery adds value precisely where PCR's structural constraints have the largest effects.
Another advantage of uHp-seq over multiplex PCR panels is that newly emerging resistance variants are readily incorporated into profiling as the genome is recovered whole, without primer redesign.
In contrast, multiplex PCR panels must be deliberately redesigned to add new targets, a slow process constrained by primer complexity in variable regions like pbp1A and rdxA.
Beyond accurate resistance genotyping, the gastric string cohort reveals that stringbased uHp-seq is not merely a less invasive alternative to endoscopic biopsy but a more comprehensive one.
By traversing the full proximal-distal axis of the stomach, the string integrates Hp populations across fundus, corpus, and antrum simultaneously.

The regional virulence and AMR heterogeneity documented in biopsy samples, where distinct cagA subtype compositions and resistance profiles were identified across gastric regions in patients with mixed-strain infections (~10% of samples), highlights that single-site sampling is inherently incomplete for characterizing the true within-host Hp landscape.

Multi-region biopsy sampling generated complete AMR profiles for all 14 patients versus single-site sampling, and the gastric string achieves the equivalent of that multi-region integration in a single procedure not requiring endoscopy.

For both virulence risk stratification and resistance-guided eradication therapy, stomach-wide sampling is clinically advantageous, and the gastric string is currently the only practical way to achieve it without endoscopy.
In this study, uHp-seq requires Hp at ≥10⁻ relative abundance to reconstruct Hp genomes, a threshold met by ~90% biopsies and string samples.

While we demonstrated uHpseq on gastric biopsies and string samples, extension to other clinically relevant sample types, including fixed gastric biopsies, gastric juice, stool, and saliva, will be optimized in future work.

Although the gastric string cohort provides informative retrospective validation of uHp-seqguided therapy selection, prospective validation studies in independent cohorts with integrated treatment-outcome data will be required to establish the clinical utility of routine deployment of uHp-seq.
Despite these constraints, uHp-seq establishes a foundation for culture-free Hp genomics, making the in vivo within-host bacterial population accessible at clinical scale.

By recovering genomes directly from host-dominated specimens, this approach opens a practical path toward precision eradication therapy, more accurate gastric cancer risk stratification, and potentially a broader framework for direct genome recovery from other clinical specimens where culture has long been the only option.

text.text: The 140-cm string was used for all samples, and the string was left in place for 1 hour prior to retrieval.
Patient height was used to estimate the distance to the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) using the manufacturer-provided formula (6.7 + 0.226 x height [cm]).
The portion of string distal to this point was used for analysis.
Hp isolation at Vanderbilt University: Hp was isolated from antral and corpus biopsies, as previously reported 76 .

text.text: Briefly, specimens were homogenized in sterile saline.
Serial dilutions were plated onto selective Trypticase Soy Agar (TSA) with 5% sheep blood.
Agar plates were incubated under microaerobic conditions at 37°C for 4 days.
Hp was confirmed by positive oxidase and urease tests and typical appearance on a Gram stain.

Hp isolation at Montefiore Medical Center: Hp culture was performed for routine clinical care at the Montefiore Medical Center Clinical Microbiology Laboratory, in accordance with standard operating procedures.

Gastric biopsy specimens were plated onto Columbia with nalidixic acid and 5% sheep blood agar plates (BD BBL, Sparks, Maryland) and incubated under microaerophilic conditions at 37°C for up to 7 days.
Identification of Hp was confirmed by positive catalase, oxidase, and rapid urease testing.

After EST, gastric antral biopsies from patients with confirmed Hp infection were cultured on blood agar (BHI + 5% sheep blood) and on a selective CVA (cefsulodin-vancomycinamphotericin B) supplemented plate, both incubated under microaerophilic conditions at 35°C. Hp and H. bilis reference strains were run in parallel on BHI plates as quality controls.
Colonies with morphology consistent with Hp were confirmed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry.
Hp isolates stock were recovered on TSA with 5% sheep blood at 37°C in 5% CO 2 for 2-3 days, all colonies were collected into one tube for DNA extraction.

Human DNA (extracted from human lymphoblastoid cell line culture) and DNA extracted from Hp-negative human stool (confirmed by both the urea breath test and stool antigen test) were used separately as background DNA.
Human DNA, Hp-negative stool DNA, and Hp26695 DNA were separately sheared to ~10 kb using g-TUBEs (Covaris, #520079).
Mock mixtures were prepared by spiking Hp26695 DNA into either human DNA or Hp-negative stool DNA at Hp DNA abundances ranging from 1 to 1.0 × 10⁻ , with a total DNA input of 1 µg per mixture.

Human, Hp, or mock DNA (200 ng -3ug) was incubated with methylation-sensitive restriction endonucleases HhaI, NlaIII, and MboI alone or combination as indicated in corresponding figures (New England Biolabs, Cat # R0139S, Cat # R0125, Cat # R0147M) at 37 °C for 30 min.
The REase was then heat-inactivated at 65 °C for 20 min, and DNA fragment size distributions were analyzed using a TapeStation or 0.9% agarose gel electrophoresis.

Input DNA was required to be high quality, pure total genomic DNA meeting the following criteria: (a) purity measured by Nanodrop, OD 260/280 of 1.8 and OD 260/230 of 2.0-2.2; (b) . average fragment size measured by electrophoresis (>10 kb); (c) Input mass measured by Qubit, ideally 200 ng in total.

Each 10 µl qPCR reaction contained 5 µl TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Cat # 4444556), 0.25 µl forward primer (OYJL234) (5'-GAGCTGTCTCAACCAGAGATT-3'), 0.25 µl reverse primer (OYJL235) (5'-GCAGTGCTAAGTTGTAGTAAAGGTC-3'), 0.125 µl probe (OYJL236) (5'-FAM/TG GAG GTG AAA TTC CTC CTA CCC G/3'-TAMRA) 77 , 10 ng template DNA and nuclease-free water.
Reactions were run on a QuantStudio 6 Flex using the fast cycling program: 50 °C for 2 min; 95 °C for 20 s; followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 1 s and 60 °C for 20 s.

text.text: Following bead beating, the homogenized tissue was divided into two 150µl aliquots.
The first aliquot was subjected to the subsequent MEM enrichment steps.

The second aliquot was processed using the QIAamp DNA Microbiome Kit (Qiagen, Cat # 51704), in which human cells remaining intact in the liquid fraction after bead beating were further selectively lysed with saponin, and the released human DNA was digested with Benzonase before bacterial cell lysis and DNA extraction.
DNA from gastric biopsy or string samples was extracted as described above, without any host DNA depletion or enrichment procedures.
ONT sequencing libraries were prepared using the Native Barcoding Kit (SQK-NBD114.24) according to the manufacturer's protocol.
Libraries were sequenced on the PromethION platform to generate sufficient sequencing depth to obtain adequate Hp reads for whole-genome assembly.

Raw ONT reads were base called and demultiplexed using Dorado (v0.4.1) 78 with the dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps_sup.cfg model for R10.4 flow cells and the emit-fast flag to produce per-barcode FASTQ files.
Barcodes yielding fewer than 10 Mb of sequence were excluded.
Sequencing statistics (total reads, read length N50, mean length) were computed using seqkit 79.

Reads were deduplicated, screened against phiX, adapter-trimmed, quality-trimmed and length-filtered (minimum 75 bp), then aligned to the Hp26695 reference genome (GCF_000307795.1, NC_018939.1; 1,667,892 bp) with Minimap2 v2.30 (-a -x sr --secondary=yes) and retained at mapping quality ≥ 30 (SAMtools v1.23).

To make samples directly comparable, each alignment was randomly downsampled to a common depth of 1,375,000 mapped reads with Picard DownsampleSam v3.4.0 (STRATEGY=Chained, ACCURACY=1e-4), and the analysis was repeated over 10 independent downsampling rounds.
At each reference position, pi was calculated from the per-base read counts as the proportion of pairwise differences among the reads covering that position.

Genome-wide pi was the mean across all reference positions, coding pi the mean across coding positions, and per-gene pi the mean across the positions of each of the 1,485 annotated genes; reported values are means across the 10 rounds.

Geographic subpopulation assignment of Hp strains was performed using two complementary approaches.
DAPC on core-genome SNPs.

Each query assembly was aligned to the Hp26695 reference with snippy (ctgs), and a core-genome SNP alignment (632,909 informative positions) was generated with snippy-core together with 1,199 geographically annotated genomes from the HpGP 28 .

text.text: Queries were projected into the discriminant space of a DAPC model pre-trained on the reference panel (200 principal components, 17-class LDA) and assigned to the nearest population centroid by Euclidean distance.

Assignment confidence was quantified as the relative margin (d2 -d1)/d2, where d1 and d2 are the distances to the top-and second-ranked centroids; margins >0.5 were classified as high confidence, 0.2-0.5 moderate, and <0.2 low.

text.text: Each assembly was queried against the pubMLST allele database by BLASTn (≥85% nucleotide identity, ≥90% allele-length coverage); the bestmatching allele per locus was selected by identity then alignment length, and the resulting profile was matched to the pubMLST sequence type (ST) table.

Because STs are not themselves informative of geographic ancestry, subpopulation was inferred by allele sharing against the HpGP reference panel of 1,200 fineSTRUCTURE-labelled genomes, typed by the identical BLASTn procedure: allelic proximity to each reference strain was defined as 1 -(fraction of commonly typed loci with different alleles), proximity was averaged within each of the 17 subpopulations, and the subpopulation with the highest mean proximity was reported with a confidence margin (difference in mean proximity between the top and runner-up subpopulation).

Virulence genes were identified from the Prokka-annotated assemblies by BLASTp (BLAST+ 2.16.0) of all predicted proteins against a reference panel of cagA (WP_267286128.1), VacA (AAD07935.1) and HtrA (AAD08063.1), with E-value < 1×10⁻ ; hits were retained at ≥70% amino-acid identity, alignment length ≥300 aa and bit score >500, and the corresponding gene and protein sequences extracted with seqkit.

text.text: Because assembly and annotation resolve only the dominant strain in a sample, all cag PAI and cagA presence/absence calls were made from reads rather than from assemblies.

Raw reads were mapped with minimap2 (-ax map-ont) to the Hp26695 reference chromosome and per-base depth and breadth computed with samtools across the cag PAI (cag1-cagA, ~547-583 kb) and across cagA, using the immediate flanking regions as a within-sample full-depth control.

Samples were called negative only when depth was 0× across the entire island while flanks retained full depth. cagA subtype (EPIYA) and vacA subtype (s1/s2, m1/m2, i1/i2/i3) was determined from assembled gene sequences in two ways:(1) alignment to established reference alleles. (2) check the feature specific sequences.

AMR-associated variants were detected at a curated panel of resistance loci targeting clarithromycin (CLR; 23S rRNA, both chromosomal copies), levofloxacin (LEV; gyrA), amoxicillin (AMX; pbp1), metronidazole (MNZ; rdxA, frxA), tetracycline (TET; 16S rRNA, both chromosomal copies, HP0399) and rifampin (RIF; rpoB) (Rifabutin is used for Hp treatment and rifampin is used for MIC test).
Detection of any mutation in the curated resistance mutation panel was considered indicative of resistance to the corresponding antibiotic.

Resistance positions were encoded in a curated BED file (see Supplementary table 8) distinguishing Tier-1 positions (allele-specific, e.g., 23S rRNA A2143G/A2144G) from Tier-2 positions (codon-level, requiring amino acid annotation to confirm pathogenicity, e.g., gyrA, rpoB).

From the total DNA extracted, targeted amplification of Hp genomic content was performed using GenoScreen's Deeplex HelP kit as per manufacturer's instructions.
The PCR amplicons were purified using AMPure XP magnetic beads (Beckman Coulter, USA) and quantified using the Qubit double-stranded DNA Broad Range Assay Kit (Invitrogen Inc.).

Following the amplicon purification, library preparation was performed using the Nextera XT Library Preparation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA) following the manufacturer's protocol with the following modifications -Hp DNA amplicons were diluted to 0.2 ng/uL in molecular grade nuclease-free water (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), for a 1 ng of DNA mass input into the library preparation workflow.
AXP magnetic beads (Beckman Coulter, USA) was used to purify the Hp DNA libraries following library amplification.
Final DNA library quantification was performed using the Qubit double-stranded High Sensitivity Assay Kit (Invitrogen Inc.).
The libraries were then normalized to a final concentration of 2 nM each and pooled.

Sequencing of these libraries was performed on the Illumina MiSeq Platform using the MiSeq v2 Micro Sequencing Kit (300 cycles; 2 x 150 bp) with 1% bacteriophage phiX control (Illumina, San Diego, CA).
Sequencing FastQ files were uploaded to GenoScreen's secure server for analysis.

Five Hp eradication regimens were considered based on the 2024 American College of Gastroenterology clinical guideline: optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT; PPI, bismuth, MNZ, and TET), rifabutin triple therapy (omeprazole, RFB, and AMX), PCAB dual therapy (vonoprazan and AMX), PCAB triple therapy (vonoprazan, CLR, and AMX), and levofloxacin triple therapy (PPI, LEV, and AMX).
Because each of these regimens contains either AMX or MNZ, resistance information for both antibiotics was required to comprehensively evaluate regimen availability.
A standard treatment regimen was considered available if all antibiotics included in the regimen were predicted to be susceptible.
Samples for which no standard regimen was identified were further classified as having no available standard regimen due to multidrug resistance or an incomplete AMR profile.
String samples were obtained from treatment-naive patients or refractory Hp patients following at least two failed eradication regimens, with clinical outcome data available.
Treatment outcome was defined by stool antigen test.
The biopsies were also collected for Hp isolation and phenotypic MIC testing. uHp-seq predicted resistance profiles were compared with phenotypic .
MIC data.
For non-RFB-containing regimens, a regimen was predicted to fail if resistance was detected to any antibiotic included in the regimen.
For RFB-containing regimens, failure was predicted only when resistance to RFB or both RFB and at least one other antibiotic in the regimen was detected.
Predicted treatment outcomes were then compared with the clinical eradication outcomes.
Sample sizes were determined by specimen availability across the contributing sites.
All genomic comparisons were paired within patients (biopsy versus matched isolate, or antrum versus corpus), so no randomization or blinding was applicable.
Samples with evidence of multistrain co-infection were excluded from the SNP category analyses as listed above; no other data were excluded.

String samples: Total DNA was extracted using the MasterPure TM Complete DNA and RNA Purification Kit (Lucigen, cat. no.
MC85200) according to manufacturer's instruction for cell samples.

Briefly, the gastric segment of the string was placed in 600µL of Tissue and Cell Lysis Solution with 2 µL of Proteinase K and vortexed briefly, after which a sterile slide was used to strip adherent fluid from the string surface.
The final DNA pellet was resuspended in 40 µL of TE buffer.

DNA (200 ng per sample) was co-digested with the methylation-sensitive restriction endonucleases HhaI, NlaIII, and MboI (New England Biolabs, Cat # R0139S, Cat # R0125, Cat # R0147M) for 90 min while fragmenting unmethylated background DNA.
Then, 1× AMPure XP (AXP) beads were used to exchange the cutting buffer into TE buffer.
Long DNA fragments were then isolated on a BluePippin (Sage Science, protocol-0.75% DF Marker S1 high pass 6-10 kb vs3) using a size window of 3 to 50 kb optimized to recover long fragment Hp DNA.

For long-read sequencing, recovered DNA was barcoded using 1µl MuA transposase (Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) Rapid Barcoding kit, RPB.114.24) prior to Nanopore sequencing on MinION or PromethION flow cells (ONT).

For short-read sequencing, libraries were prepared either by Tn5-mediated tagmentation directly following size selection or by amplification from the long-read barcoded product and sequenced on Illumina platforms NovaSeq 6000.
